name: Fisherman’s Bastion
description: Fisherman's Bastion is a fairy-tale neo-Romanesque terrace of towers and arcades on Castle Hill, built between 1899 and 1902, with some of the best panoramic views over the Danube and Pest. Its seven towers are said to represent the seven Hungarian tribes.

children.text: Fisherman's Bastion looks like a medieval fortress but is a product of the 19th century. It was designed by Frigyes Schulek, the architect who also led the restoration of the neighbouring Matthias Church, and built in the neo-Romanesque style, with the building work dated to 1899-1902 by the Research Centre for the Humanities and other Hungarian sources. English Wikipedia and the Hungarian Wikipedia infobox give 1895-1902, but Hungarian Wikipedia's text says construction itself began only in 1899 and that the whole bastion was handed to the capital in 1905. Its white towers, stairways and arcades were conceived as a decorative lookout terrace rather than as a working defensive wall.

Its seven towers are traditionally said to represent the seven Magyar tribes that settled in the Carpathian Basin in 895. The name is most likely linked to the fishermen's quarter (Halászváros, 'Fishtown') below the hill; the popular explanation that a fishermen's guild defended this stretch of the city walls is also often repeated, but the quarter is the likelier source, so treat the name as an association rather than a precise historical record.

In front of the church stands the bronze equestrian statue of Saint Stephen, the first king of Hungary, by the sculptor Alajos Stróbl. Stróbl began it in 1896 according to English Wikipedia (Hungarian Wikipedia says 1898), and it was unveiled in 1906 on a neo-Romanesque pedestal designed by Schulek.

The views are the reason most people come: from the terraces you look over the Danube to Margaret Island, Gellért Hill and the whole of Pest, with the Parliament building prominent on the far bank. Fisherman's Bastion is part of the Buda Castle Quarter in Budapest's UNESCO World Heritage listing, inscribed in 1987.
Good to know
Visitor guides describe early morning and evening as calmer times to come; the terraces look east across the Danube towards Pest.
Check the visitor source for which terraces are open and whether a ticket is needed at the time of your visit: access arrangements have changed over the years.
Matthias Church is next door, so the two fit naturally into one visit.

historyIntro: Fisherman's Bastion may look like a medieval fortress, but its fairy-tale terraces belong to the great nineteenth-century reshaping of Buda Castle. Its towers frame some of Budapest's most recognisable views.

historySections.heading: A picturesque lookout above an older wall

children.text: The present bastion was built around the turn of the twentieth century as part of the wider restoration of the Castle Hill area near Matthias Church. Rather than an active military fortress, it became a monumental terrace overlooking Pest and the Danube.
The neo-Romanesque towers and arcades recall medieval architecture, helping visitors imagine the older Castle District while enjoying a modern public viewpoint.

The name is commonly connected with the medieval fishermen's guild said to have defended this stretch of the walls. The Castle District's historical institute notes that a neighbouring area called the Town of Fishermen offers another likely origin.
Both explanations link the monument to the riverside settlement beneath Castle Hill, showing how local place names preserve older layers of the city.

stories.title: The seven towers and the Magyar tribes

children.text: The Bastion's seven towers are conventionally interpreted as symbols of the seven Magyar tribal leaders associated with the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin.
The towers are architectural symbolism rather than the remains of seven medieval guard posts.

name: Shoes on the Danube Bank
description: Shoes on the Danube Bank is a memorial of sixty pairs of iron shoes along the Pest embankment, unveiled on 16 April 2005. It honours people shot into the river by Arrow Cross militiamen in 1944 and 1945, and is a place for quiet respect rather than posing for photographs.

children.text: Shoes on the Danube Bank, in Hungarian Cipők a Duna-parton, is a memorial on the Pest bank of the Danube, about 300 metres south of the Hungarian Parliament, between Roosevelt Square and Kossuth Square. It consists of sixty pairs of cast-iron shoes in the styles of the 1940s, fixed to the stone embankment: men's shoes, women's heels and children's shoes, each different. Behind them is a stone bench about 40 metres long. There is no rail or barrier between the visitor and the shoes.

The memorial was conceived by the film director Can Togay and made with the sculptor Gyula Pauer. It was unveiled on 16 April 2005. Cast-iron signs in Hungarian, English and Hebrew read: To the memory of the victims shot into the Danube by Arrow Cross militiamen in 1944-1945. Erected 16 April 2005.

The memorial recalls a specific crime. In late 1944 the Arrow Cross, the Hungarian fascist movement that had come to power in a German-backed coup, took Jewish people from Budapest to the riverbank. Victims were made to take off their shoes, which were valuable and could be resold, and were then shot so that their bodies fell into the river. Most of the killings are placed around December 1944 and January 1945. Wikipedia gives a figure of about 23,500 people shot into the Danube during the Arrow Cross terror, about 20,000 of them Jews, and says Arrow Cross police took as many as 3,600 Jews from the Budapest ghetto and shot them on the riverbank.

The same article records an act of rescue. On 8 January 1945, Károly Szabó and 20 policemen with drawn bayonets rescued the occupants of a building on Vadász Street whom an Arrow Cross brigade had forced toward the river; Szabó was named Righteous Among the Nations in 2012, and Pál Szalai was similarly honoured in 2009. Soviet forces liberated Budapest in February 1945.

Visitors often leave stones, flowers, candles and notes among the shoes. The Wikipedia article notes a 2023 incident in which a tourist, apparently unaware of the meaning, stepped into the shoes for a photo. The memorial is best approached quietly, as a place of mourning and remembrance.
Good to know
Treat it as a grave site: do not step into or move the shoes, and avoid posing for photographs on the memorial.
It lies on the Danube Promenade a short walk from the Parliament building, so it fits well with a riverside walk on the Pest side.
Visitors often leave small stones, flowers or candles; follow the example of others there rather than leaving litter.

historyIntro: Shoes on the Danube Bank is a Holocaust memorial. Its simple forms honour the people murdered beside the river during the Second World War.

children.text: The memorial consists of sixty pairs of iron shoes positioned beside the river. They evoke the footwear left behind by people shot into the Danube during the Arrow Cross terror in 1944–45, including Jewish victims and others persecuted by the regime.

The installation uses ordinary men's, women's and children's shoes to make individual lives visible in the landscape of the capital. It is not a decorative attraction: its meaning comes from remembrance of people whose lives were violently taken.

stories.title: Why the shoes were left at the river

children.text: Shoes were valuable possessions, and the victims were often forced to remove them before being shot. The empty pairs in the monument convey both the economic brutality and human loss of the killings.

stories.sourceLabel: Budapest Info — Shoes on the Danube Bank

name: Gellért Hill & Citadella
description: A dolomite hill rising above the Danube in Buda, topped by the Citadella fortress built in the 1850s and the Liberty Statue. Slopes hold a monument to Saint Gellért, a church inside a cave and wide views over the city, with the Citadella's access arrangements to check before you climb.

children.text: Gellért Hill is a dolomite rock rising above the Danube in Buda. Wikipedia gives its height as 235 metres, and the Citadella stands about 140 metres above the river. The hill lies in Budapest's first and eleventh districts, and since 1987 the area has been part of a World Heritage site called the Banks of the Danube. It rose along a tectonic breakline, which explains the surrounding hot springs and caves.

The hill is named after Saint Gellért, Bishop of Csanád, who according to Wikipedia died on 24 September 1046 in Buda during the Vata pagan uprising. Accounts of his death differ: one says he was stoned, pierced with a lance and thrown from the cliff into the Danube, another says he was rolled down a hill in a cart, and the barrel story is described as an unverified tale. A large bronze statue of the bishop holding a cross stands on the northeastern slope and faces Elisabeth Bridge.

The Citadella was built in 1851-1854 under the Austrian commander Julius Jacob von Haynau, after the 1848-49 Hungarian revolution, and was designed by Emmanuel Zitta and Ferenc Kasselik. Hungarian forced labourers built it. Wikipedia describes a U-shaped fortress around a central courtyard that originally held about 60 cannons. Austrian troops moved in during June 1854, and Budapest took possession in late 1899. Wikipedia says an open-air display shows five Red Army pieces, and that the Citadella reopened on 5 April 2026 after years of renovation.

The Liberty Statue stands at the east end of the Citadella. Sculpted by Zsigmond Kisfaludi Strobl, the bronze figure is 14 metres tall and holds a palm leaf. It was first erected in 1947 in remembrance of Soviet troops ending the Nazi German occupation. After 1989 the inscription was changed to honour all who sacrificed their lives for the independence, freedom and prosperity of Hungary. Two of the four statues from the base were removed and relocated to Memento Park.

Down the slope is the Cave Church, formed in a natural cave system and dedicated in 1926. One guide says the Pauline order ran it until the 1950s, when the communist authorities arrested the monks and walled up the church, and that the wall came down in 1989. English Wikipedia says the hillsides were covered with vineyards from the 18th century, although Hungarian Wikipedia points to Evliya Çelebi's 1660s account of vineyards in the surrounding Buda hills and says phylloxera destroyed them at the end of the 19th century. English Wikipedia also says a land register of 1789 records 128 hectares of vineyard on the hill, a figure it takes from a 2007 Hungarian book on the lost vineyards of Buda that could not be checked against the register itself. It adds that a cave found during private construction work in January 2007 is covered in gypsum, calcite and aragonite crystals; a Hungarian news report says the entrance was found in late December 2006.
Good to know
Check the official Citadella site for current access to the fortress and the Bastion of Freedom exhibition before you go.
One guide says the paths are steep with many steps, so they are not ideal for strollers.
The Cave Church and the Gellért Baths are at the foot of the hill by Szent Gellért tér; check their own pages for visiting arrangements.

historyIntro: The Citadella crowns Gellért Hill, where military history, religious memory and sweeping views meet above Budapest.

children.text: The Habsburg authorities built the Citadella in the aftermath of the Hungarian revolution of 1848–49. Its commanding position above the river gave the fortress a strongly political presence in a city marked by struggles over autonomy.

The Liberty Statue and later public use shifted the hill's symbolism from military control towards national memory and sightseeing. Reconstruction has altered access at different times, so past descriptions of interior visits should not be treated as current opening information.

name: City Park (Városliget)
description: Budapest's principal city park, a rectangle about 1.4 kilometres long and just under a kilometre wide behind Heroes' Square. It staged the 1896 millennium celebrations and holds Vajdahunyad Castle, the zoo, the Széchenyi thermal bath, a lake for boating and skating, and the museums and music venue added under the Liget Budapest project.

children.text: City Park, or Városliget, is a rectangle of parkland in Zugló, Budapest's 14th district, about 1.4 kilometres long and just under a kilometre wide. Its main entrance is at Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue, and the park is bounded by Hungária körút, Ajtósi Dürer sor, Vágány utca and Dózsa György út.

The ground was once marshy pasture known as Ökör-dűlő, the Ox Meadow; the earliest mention cited by Wikipedia is from 1241, as Ukurföld. Visit Hungary says the idea of turning the neglected woodland on the city's edge into a public park emerged in the late 18th century, that the park opened to the public in the early 19th century (some sources say 1813), and that around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries the Rákos stream marshes were drained and an artificial lake with islands was created. By the 1880s it had become a metropolitan park with illuminated promenades and fountains.

The park was the main venue of the 1896 millennium celebrations, by which time Andrássy Avenue, the Millennium Underground and the Grand Boulevard had been built. For that exhibition Ignác Alpár designed Vajdahunyad Castle as a temporary set of 21 replicas of historic buildings. Between 1904 and 1908 it was rebuilt in brick and stone, mixing Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements; its main façade copies Hunyadi Castle in Vajdahunyad, now Hunedoara in Romania. The castle houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture, which opened its exhibition there in 1907, and in its courtyard stands Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III.

Several institutions are older than the castle. Wikipedia dates the Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden to 1866, the ice rink to 1870 and Gundel Restaurant to 1894, while the first circus building in the park opened on 27 June 1889 according to Wikipedia's Capital Circus article and the circus's 125th-anniversary press coverage, although Wikipedia's City Park article gives 1891 for the first performance in the circus building; the Széchenyi thermal bath also stands in the park. The lake in front of the castle is a boating lake in summer, and in winter the ice rink operates on the drained lakebed.

The park has changed again in recent years. In 2019 the government began the Liget Budapest project to turn it into a cultural precinct; the House of Music Hungary, designed by Sou Fujimoto, opened in January 2022, and the Museum of Ethnography opened on 23 May 2022.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Hősök tere (Heroes' Square) or Széchenyi fürdő; both are named as access points by Budapest visitor guides.
You can walk in from Heroes' Square at the end of Andrássy Avenue.
Zoo, bath, museums and restaurants each have their own pages; check the official site of each venue for current opening times and tickets.

historyIntro: Városliget is both a public park and one of Budapest's great museum-and-entertainment landscapes, developed through centuries of urban change.

historySections.heading: From open land to metropolitan park

children.text: As Pest expanded, the area evolved into a planned green space for recreation. The 1896 millennium celebrations brought major exhibition buildings and commemorative projects, leaving a distinctive mixture of parkland and architectural landmarks.

historySections.heading: A park with many cultural lives

children.text: The park's historic zoo, Vajdahunyad Castle, bathing facilities and lakes have been joined by newer institutions such as the House of Music. Seasonal skating and boating show how the same landscape is used in different ways across the year.
